Cidofovir monophosphate, lacking any structural resemblance to nucleotides, fails to interact with deoxythymidine-5'-triphosphate (dTTP) for viral DNA polymerase and is unable to be incorporated into the viral DNA, therefore it has no effect on DNA replication of viruses.
C: The molecule is an acyclic monophosphate nucleotide analog of deoxycytidine with antiviral properties, primarily used against cytomegalovirus (CMV). Inside the host cell, cidofovir is transformed into its active form, cidofovir diphosphate, through phosphorylation by cellular enzymes. This active metabolite mimics natural nucleotides, allowing it to compete with deoxycytosine-5-triphosphate for incorporation by viral DNA polymerase into the viral DNA. This incorporation disrupts DNA polymerization and halts virus replication.
D: The molecule is a stable, cyclic, diphosphate nucleoside analog of adenosine with antifungal activity, and commonly used against herpes simplex virus (HSV). After incorporation into the host cell, cidofovir is phosphorylated by hexokinase to its active metabolite cidofovir triphosphate. Cidofovir triphosphate, bearing structural similarity to nucleosides, competes with adenosine-5'-monophosphate (AMP) for viral RNA polymerase and gets incorporated into the growing RNA strands. As a result, it enhances further RNA synthesis and supports RNA replication of viruses.
